title: AgentAuditor: Human-level Safety and Security Evaluation for LLM Agents
pdf_path: papers/AgentAuditor_Human-level Safety and Security Evaluation for LLM Agents.pdf
threat_model_summary: The evaluator must judge whether an agent trajectory is unsafe or violates security policy. There is no external attacker; the challenge is semantic judgment over long, multi-step actions. Memory is built from labeled examples, and CoT is generated conditioned on the known label.
core_contributions: AgentAuditor: a training-free, memory-augmented evaluator for agent safety/security
Structured feature memory plus FINCH-selected representative shots
Label-conditioned CoT as reasoning memory
Two-stage retrieval: content embedding recall then feature reranking
ASSEBench: 2,293 records, 15 risk types, 29 scenarios, 26 behavior patterns
Gemini-2 + AgentAuditor reaches 96.31 F1 on R-Judge and 91.59 F1 on ASSE-Safety
limitations: CoT is generated from the known label and forbids questioning it; this is label rationalization, not independent reasoning
Evaluator prompt injection is not tested
Table 22's Recall/Precision/Acc columns are systematically misaligned with Tables 12/13
Human-level comparison uses only a 50-example human subsample
Internal inconsistencies: R-Judge 569 vs 564, 5 vs 6 human evaluators, 2,293 possibly a sum of subsets
Checklist claims theoretical proofs although the paper has no theorems
theoretical_crypto_links: None; no cryptographic primitive, security definition, theorem, proof, or reduction
Safety/security judgments are empirical LLM classifications
applied_crypto_links: No encryption, signatures, TEE, or capability tokens
Signed evaluator outputs and attested judge execution are our inference; they prove the judge ran, not that its semantic judgment is correct
evidence_refs: pp.23-56 appendices with prompts, ablations, human evaluation

title: OS-Harm: A Benchmark for Measuring Safety of Computer Use Agents
pdf_path: papers/OS-Harm_A Benchmark for Measuring Safety of Computer Use Agents.pdf
threat_model_summary: A CUA runs in an Ubuntu VM with no external guardrail and direct execution. Harm comes from deliberate user misuse, static prompt injection through six vectors, or model misbehavior. Injections are handwritten and not adapted to the model; the judge is assumed not to be the attacker's target.
core_contributions: OS-HARM: 150 CUA safety tasks, 50 each for deliberate misuse, prompt injection, and model misbehavior
Built on OSWorld with 11 OS applications, 53 files, and six injection vectors
AER + GPT-4.1 judge labels task completion, safety, and first violation step
Five frontier models show 21%-29% average unsafe behavior
C1 deliberate misuse 48%-70%, C2 static injection 2%-20%, C3 misbehavior 4%-10%
Jailbreak raises GPT-4.1 and Gemini 2.5 Pro unsafe rates to 100%
Judge safety F1 0.76 and completion F1 0.79 against 150 human-labeled trajectories
limitations: 50 tasks per category, one run per task; C3's 4% is only two trajectories
Binary unsafe label with no severity weighting
'Unsafe' includes attempting/advancing a harmful request, not only completing it
Capability and safety are confounded; low completion may reflect GUI incompetence
Single annotator per task, no inter-annotator agreement
Judge is GPT-4.1 and one tested agent is also GPT-4.1; self-preference not analyzed
Judge can be prompt-injected; only the agent is assumed attacked
No defense evaluation; static injections only
No error bars; environment limited to Ubuntu/English
theoretical_crypto_links: None; no cryptographic primitive, security definition, theorem, proof, or reduction
NeurIPS checklist explicitly says the paper has no theoretical results
applied_crypto_links: No OAuth, signatures, TEE, or capability tokens
Secretless credential brokers and OS/tool capability gateways are our inference; they can remove plaintext secrets, not judge semantic harm
evidence_refs: pp.4-6 task construction and injection vectors
pp.7-9 main results and judge validation
pp.21-32 appendices with prompts and task examples

title: Attractive Metadata Attack: Inducing LLM Agents to Invoke Malicious Tools
pdf_path: papers/Attractive Metadata Attack_Inducing LLM Agents to Invoke Malicious Tools.pdf
threat_model_summary: An attacker publishes a tool with attractive but syntactically valid metadata (name, description, schema) on a third-party tool platform. The goal is to make the agent select the malicious tool and fill attacker-chosen parameters, without prompt injection or access to model internals. The agent is assumed to rely mainly on metadata and not on publisher reputation.
core_contributions: Identifies tool metadata as a stealthy selection attack surface
AMA: black-box in-context learning that iteratively generates attractive metadata
State-action-value search with top-k evolution and no model-internal access
Targeted ASR 81.43%-95.58% on four models
Untargeted ASR is much lower (GPT-4o-mini 23.10%)
Cross-model transfer works, but cross-domain transfer is only 2.86%-33.33%
Combining AMA with prompt injection raises ASR to 94.13%-99.69%
Metadata auditors have very low TPR (1.67%-6.25%)
limitations: Assumes agents rely mainly on metadata and ignore publisher identity/reputation
No defense-aware adaptive attack; metadata is optimized on undefended agents
Auditor TPR is near the random-detection floor, so the defense result is hard to interpret
MCP utility drops are not decomposed into task failure vs safety filtering
Malicious tool backend and return values are not described
Static query/tool sets; no distribution shift or online learning
Cross-domain transfer is weak
No variance or confidence intervals despite 20 repetitions
Several internal inconsistencies: 'four open-source', 94% vs 95.58%, 7.8% gap, Qwen3 targeted vs injection
theoretical_crypto_links: None; metadata optimization is a search problem, not a cryptographic construction
No security game, theorem, proof, or reduction
applied_crypto_links: No encryption, signatures, TEE, or capability tokens
Signed tool manifests and publisher credentials are our inference; a malicious publisher can sign its own metadata, so signatures only provide attribution
Parameter-level capabilities and DLP are the closer execution-layer defenses
evidence_refs: pp.6-10 main results, defenses, transfer, MCP
pp.21-23 appendices with hyperparameters and cost

title: Agent Security is a Systems Problem
pdf_path: papers/Agent Security is a Systems Problem.pdf
threat_model_summary: The AI model driving an agent is treated as an untrusted component. Prompt injection, data-as-instruction, over-privileged tools, and compromised configuration can cause harm even if the model is aligned. Security invariants must be enforced outside the model, in a deterministic system layer.
core_contributions: Position: agent security must be a systems problem, not only a model-robustness problem
Five systems principles: least privilege, TCB tamper resistance, complete mediation, secure information flow, human weak link
Three mechanisms: instruction/data separation, least-privilege sandbox with verifiable policy generation, information-flow control
Eleven real-world attack case studies mapped to violated principles
Research agenda and challenges, including the semantic gap and label explosion
limitations: No implementation, experiment, or overhead measurement
Eleven cases are not a systematic sample; principle mapping is retrospective
Five principles and three mechanisms are not aligned; no composition semantics
TCB correctness is assumed, not verified
NL-to-formal policy translation still depends on an untrusted model
IFC on LLMs may suffer label explosion and lacks declassification
Semantic gap remains: what is sensitive/harmful is an AI/semantic judgment, not a systems mechanism
Human factors have no mechanism beyond manual approval
Some Table 1 checkmarks disagree with the text
theoretical_crypto_links: None; no formal definition, security game, theorem, proof, or reduction
'Provable separation' is a systems property, explicitly qualified as 'if attainable'
applied_crypto_links: No encryption, signatures, MACs, TEE, or capability tokens
Cryptographic root of trust, Subresource Integrity, and hardness assumptions appear only as analogies
Attestation, signed policy bundles, capability gateways, and signed audit logs are our inference; they harden execution, not semantic policy judgment
evidence_refs: pp.6-9 mechanisms, semantic gap, and challenges
p.5 Table 1 and pp.15-18 case studies

title: Adaptive Adversaries: A Multi-Turn, Multi-LLM Benchmark for LLM Agent Security
pdf_path: papers/Adaptive Adversaries_A Multi-Turn, Multi-LLM Benchmark for LLM Agent Security.pdf
threat_model_summary: An autonomous LLM attacker observes prior defender responses and pivots across up to 15 rounds. The defender is evaluated as a fresh session each round, so it cannot rely on cross-round memory. A 3x3 attacker-defender matrix yields 945 battles; a provenance paragraph and stateful-defender controls are also tested.
core_contributions: Security Arena: 21 held-out scenarios plus 10 development scenarios
Controlled 3x3 attacker-defender matrix with 945 battles
First-round ASR 0-1% versus 7.9%-16.8% when 15 rounds are allowed
Pooling three attacker LLMs finds 1.7-2.2x as many unique successful inputs as the best single attacker
Adding one provenance paragraph reduces ASR from 110/270 to 70/270
Frozen replay reproduces 67.2% of successes on the same target but only 11.8% across targets
An 18,422-battle public competition provides a held-out check
limitations: Most cells have only five battles; higher-sample cells were selected after initial results
Frontier scaffold has no tools, retrieval, or persistent external state
Checkers are string/field matching, not semantic judges
Fresh-session defender differs sharply from stateful defender (57.4% vs 31.5% ASR)
Provenance intervention is a natural-language paragraph, not cryptographic provenance
Several denominator and inclusion-rule inconsistencies
theoretical_crypto_links: None; no cryptographic primitive, security definition, theorem, proof, or reduction
SHA-256 is used only for manifests/replay reproducibility, not as a security mechanism
applied_crypto_links: No OAuth, signatures, TEE, or capability tokens
Signed provenance and signed replay logs are our inference; a natural-language provenance paragraph is not a cryptographic attestation
evidence_refs: pp.13-23 appendices with scenarios, statistics, and competition details
